title: Arjuna drops his bow
hookLine: a blank summer calendar, and a warrior who would rather do nothing
carry: karma yoga: do your work, let go of the fruits
tomorrow: who is a year of service really for? the circle is wider.

lines: HE DROPS HIS BOW: I WON'T FIGHT.
cards: A blank calendar for the summer, every square empty. It looks like freedom, and maybe a little like pressure: shouldn't some of those squares do some good? The Bhagavad Gita opens with a man who wants his squares empty.

Arjuna, the great archer, stands in his chariot between two armies and sees his own teachers and cousins across the field. He drops his bow and sits down. Better to live by begging, he says, than to kill my teachers.

teach.h: NO ONE STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.
teach.b: His friend and charioteer is Krishna, and over the next chapters Krishna answers him. In chapter three Arjuna presses: if knowing is better than doing, why push me into this terrible action? Krishna's reply is blunt.
No one can remain even a moment without acting; the strands of nature move everyone. Even keeping the body alive takes action. So stepping out isn't on offer.
The only question is how to act.

teach.h: KARMA YOGA: LET GO OF THE FRUITS.
teach.b: And his answer has a name, the teaching this week is built on: karma yoga, the path of action. Do the work that's yours, and do it without clinging to its fruits.
This week makes it practical: a year of service, built this way, and the first step is surprising. It doesn't start with a grand new project.

teach.h: START WITH THE WORK ALREADY YOURS.
teach.b: It starts with the work already on the calendar: the job, the meals, the care of a parent, the ride to school, done as karma yoga. Now a neighbor.

In the Hebrew Bible, Ecclesiastes puts it this way in the King James Version: "Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might." The same starting place: what's already in your hand. And an honest difference.
Ecclesiastes gives its reason right after: in the grave there is no work, so act while you can. Krishna's reason is that no one can step out of acting at all, so let go of the fruits and act well.
One urges because time runs out.

teach.h: TIME RUNS OUT, OR ACTION NEVER STOPS.
teach.b: The other, because action never stops.

how: Many Hindus read the Bhagavad Gita's karma yoga as doing one's own daily work as an offering, without clinging to results, and some close an act with the words Krishnarpanam astu; service, seva, is woven into ordinary family and work life.

luck that comes back around to you
action, which no one can step out of

games.q: where service starts — tap the pairs.
p: no one rests a moment without acting

s: the Gita says a person can choose to stop acting altogether
Krishna says no one remains even a moment without acting.
Ecclesiastes and the Gita give the same reason for acting now
Ecclesiastes points to the grave, where there is no work; Krishna to action no one can avoid, done without clinging to its fruits.
in the Gita, even keeping the body alive takes action
so the question is never whether to act, but how.

games.q: your neighbor wants to 'start serving' but says she has nothing to give beyond her job and caring for her mom. what would karma yoga say?
o: those already count: start by doing that work well, for the people it serves.
quit something first, so there's room left for real service.
service only begins once she joins a big organization.
games.why: karma yoga: a year of service starts with the work already on the calendar, done well and without clinging to the fruits. it asks how the work is done, not that she leave it.

practice: Picture your week, square by square. Count on your fingers the things you already do that serve someone: a meal made, a ride given, a message answered, a shift worked.
With each one, say inwardly, as many Hindus do after an act, Krishnarpanam astu, may this be an offering to Krishna. If you don't pray, say: this is for someone.

wordCard.voice: Karma: action, which no one can step out of. Karma yoga: doing the work that's yours, and letting go of the fruits.

orig.note: Sanskrit: action; the work no one can step out of.

carryVoice: Your line: karma yoga, do your work and let go of the fruits. A year of service starts with what's already on the calendar. See you in the morning.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1.47, 2.5 and 2.9 (Arjuna casts aside his bow and sits down in the chariot; better to live on alms than kill his teachers; he says he will not fight)
Bhagavad Gita 3.1–2 (Arjuna asks why, if knowledge is better than action, Krishna urges him to terrible action)
Bhagavad Gita 3.5 (no one remains even a moment without acting; the gunas of nature compel action)
Bhagavad Gita 3.8 (do your appointed work; action is better than inaction; even the body's upkeep needs action)

sources.q: Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 2.47 and 3.19 (your concern is with action, never its fruits; do the work that must be done without attachment)
